title: Edmund and the Bell
premise: Urban explorer Gideon Vasquez discovers unmapped tunnels beneath the town of Harrow's Bend, where a bronze bell that vanished in 1974 still hangs, ringing for no one. When their childhood imaginary friend, Edmund, appears on the porch unchanged after thirty years, Gideon learns Edmund is not imaginary but a ward — a child taken by the bell's keepers and bound to it, his identity slowly consumed with each tolling. The tunnels are the bell's throat, and every generation of Harrow's Bend has fed it a child to keep the harvest plentiful; Gideon's own family took something from the bell in 1974 and has been paying interest ever since. To free Edmund and end the debt, Gideon must descend before the harvest moon rises, return what was stolen — the bell's clapper, hidden in their grandmother's house — and choose whether to take the keepers' place or let the bell fall silent forever.
about_author: Mara Thornbury is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing small-town municipal records across the American Midwest, where she collected more unexplained disappearances than she ever reported. She writes horror about the debts families hide in basements, attics, and bloodlines.

chapters.title: The Doors All Counted
chapters.summary: Gideon Vasquez, methodical urban explorer, maps storm drains beneath Harrow's Bend and finds a tunnel that appears on no survey, its walls scored with tally marks. POV: Gideon. Beat: unease seeded by competence — the moment routine curiosity tips into wrongness.

chapters.title: A Sound Like a Held Breath
chapters.summary: Deep in the tunnel Gideon hears a single low tone, feels it in their teeth, and flees without photographing anything — breaking their own rules. That night they check the survey archives: the tunnel was sealed in 1974. POV: Gideon. Beat: denial hardening into obsession.

chapters.title: Edmund on the Porch
chapters.summary: Gideon returns home to find Edmund — their childhood imaginary friend, a boy in a yellow raincoat — sitting on the porch steps, unchanged at eight years old while Gideon is nearly forty. He says he waited where they left him. POV: Gideon. Beat: uncanny tenderness laced with dread.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Kept Locked
chapters.summary: Gideon visits their grandmother Ruth, whose reaction to Edmund's name is terror. She reveals fragments: 1974, her brother Thomas, a bargain made beneath the church, and a box she refuses to open. POV: alternating Gideon and Ruth. Beat: inheritance revealed as burden.

chapters.title: The Bell That Isn't There
chapters.summary: Town records show Harrow's Bend's church bell was removed in 1974, yet older parishioners cross themselves when Gideon asks about 'the ringing.' Edmund grows agitated whenever bells appear — doorbells, wind chimes, phone alarms. POV: Gideon. Beat: the town's complicity surfaces.

chapters.title: Tally Marks in Fresh Chalk
chapters.summary: Gideon re-enters the tunnel and finds new tally marks beside the old ones — hundreds more, some still wet. A child's voice counts somewhere ahead in the dark. They retreat, but the exit opens onto the tunnel mouth again, three times. POV: Gideon. Beat: the labyrinth claims them.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession, Part One
chapters.summary: Ruth admits the Vasquez family were keepers: each generation guards the clapper and chooses the tithe. In 1974 it was Thomas's turn to be given, but Ruth hid the clapper instead, hoping to starve the bell. It took someone else's child instead. POV: Ruth. Beat: guilt as generational wound.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Wasn't Borrowed
chapters.summary: Edmund confesses he is real: Edmund Pryce, taken in 1974 as the substitute tithe, bound to the bell, sustained only by Gideon's childhood belief. Each year he remembers less of himself. He doesn't blame Gideon — which is worse. POV: Edmund. Beat: heartbreak; stakes become personal.

chapters.title: The Keepers' Choir
chapters.summary: At night Gideon dreams of robed figures in the tunnel, faces like wet clay, singing the bell awake. Waking, they find clay under their own fingernails. The keepers are recruiting a replacement keeper — and they've chosen Gideon. POV: Gideon. Beat: identity begins eroding.

chapters.title: Missing Since Tuesday
chapters.summary: A local girl, Dana Okafor, vanishes; searchers comb the fields as the harvest moon approaches. Gideon realizes the bell, starved since Ruth hid the clapper, is taking irregular tithes now — hungrier and less careful. POV: Gideon and Dana briefly. Beat: clock starts ticking; moral weight lands.

chapters.title: The Box Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Ruth finally opens the box: the clapper, wrapped in christening cloth, cold enough to burn. She begs Gideon to bury it deeper, to let the bell starve even if it costs strays like Dana. Gideon refuses. POV: Ruth and Gideon. Beat: the thematic fault line — safety versus justice.

chapters.title: What the Bell Shows You
chapters.summary: Touching the clapper, Gideon visions the bell's memory: generations of children, the keepers' original bargain for a dying harvest, and Thomas Vasquez alive inside the bell, grown old without aging out. The bell doesn't kill; it keeps. Forever. POV: Gideon. Beat: horror deepens — captivity worse than death.

chapters.title: Edmund Forgets His Name
chapters.summary: Edmund fails to recognize the yellow raincoat, then briefly forgets Gideon. Belief is failing as Gideon's own identity frays under the keepers' pull. Gideon writes Edmund's story down to anchor him. POV: Gideon. Beat: love expressed as record-keeping; quiet devastation.

chapters.title: The Church Basement Ledger
chapters.summary: In the deconsecrated church, Gideon finds the keepers' ledger: every tithe since 1891, names in a child's handwriting, including Dana Okafor's — entered two days before she vanished. The ledger lists one name left blank: the next keeper. POV: Gideon. Beat: dread of predestination.

chapters.title: They Offer You the Robe
chapters.summary: The keepers come to Gideon openly, offering the choice: take the robe, keep the town safe, feed the bell on schedule — or refuse and watch it take wildly. They show Gideon a vision of Harrow's Bend starving, then burning. POV: Gideon. Beat: temptation articulated; power's corruption made explicit.

chapters.title: Dana in the Walls
chapters.summary: Following the ledger's logic, Gideon finds Dana alive inside the tunnel walls, kept in a pocket of ringing silence, half-transformed. She begs not to be left. Freeing her means unbinding the bell entirely — no more bargains, no more protection. POV: Gideon and Dana. Beat: resolve crystallizes.

chapters.title: Ruth's Last Tally
chapters.summary: Ruth, dying, gives Gideon the truth she withheld: Thomas could have been freed all along; freeing a tithe requires a keeper to surrender their name in exchange. She hid the clapper to avoid paying that price. She asks forgiveness. POV: Ruth. Beat: reckoning with cowardice; theme of inheritance completed.

chapters.title: Descent on the Harvest Moon
chapters.summary: As the moon rises, Gideon descends with the clapper, Edmund, and Ruth's confession written in their own hand. The tunnel breathes; the tally marks glow. The keepers line the passage, singing. Gideon walks toward the bell without counting doors for the first time. POV: Gideon. Beat: surrender of control; courage as letting go.

chapters.title: The Return
chapters.summary: At the bell, Gideon offers the clapper and demands the return of what was taken: Thomas, Edmund, Dana. The keepers counter — one name freely given keeps the balance. Gideon begins to speak their own name, and Edmund screams for them to stop. POV: Gideon. Beat: climax; sacrifice poised on a knife edge.

chapters.title: The Name Given Back
chapters.summary: Edmund intervenes: as a tithe already belonging to the bell, his name can close the ledger — he chooses oblivion over eternity, giving himself back willingly. The bell tolls once, cracks, and releases its kept ones. Thomas steps out an old man; Dana wakes whole. POV: Edmund, then Gideon. Beat: climax resolved through agency, not force.

chapters.title: After the Ringing Stopped
chapters.summary: The tunnels collapse; the keepers crumble to clay. Gideon, half-erased from the town's records and memories, rebuilds themselves piece by piece with Edmund's help — Edmund now mortal, aging, remembering. Ruth dies at peace. The town's harvest fails once, then recovers. POV: Gideon. Beat: grief braided with renewal.

chapters.title: Doors Left Open
chapters.summary: One year later, Gideon publishes nothing, maps nothing, but leaves the porch light on and the front door unlocked. On the anniversary, children in Harrow's Bend report an imaginary friend who tells them to count the doors and always leave one open. Gideon smiles, and does not correct them. POV: Gideon. Beat: resolution — power renounced, identity chosen, inheritance rewritten.
